What is meant is the perishing of his whole person, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿because of what your hands have sent forward﴾. The meaning of "wa tabba" is: that occurred and came about, as in the poet's saying:

"May God repay him with the worst of his recompense, the recompense of the snarling dogs, and he has indeed done it."

[It is as if he had done him a good turn, so he repaid him with evil, and so he invoked against him by saying: "May God repay him with the worst of his recompense." "And he has indeed done it" means: God did that recompense in reality, since He brought it about. In it is one of the types of rhetorical ornament:

It is also narrated, in place of the first half-line: "May his Lord repay 'Adi ibn Hatim on my behalf." It is also said that the returning pronoun is the recompense understood from "jaza." It is also narrated, in place of the first half-line as well: "May God repay 'Abs, the 'Abs of the family of Bughayd." This is a well-known tribe, and the poet is probably someone else. What some commentators on the shawahid of al-Jami have related, that 'Adi ibn Hatim was a man who had built a palace for al-Nu'man ibn Imru' al-Qays on the outskirts of Kufa, and he was impressed by it, so he asked him: "Have you built one like it?" He said: "No, and I built it on a stone; if it fell, the palace would fall," so he threw him from its top and he fell dead, is an error. The correct view is that this story actually happened to Sinimmar, who is mentioned in the saying:

"His sons repaid Abu al-Ghaylan, out of arrogance, and good deeds are repaid as Sinimmar was repaid."

For 'Adi ibn Hatim was a companion from the core of the Arabs; and the pronoun "his sons" refers to Abu al-Ghaylan with a kasra. Sinimmar is with two kasras and then a shadda.

"'An" (from/on account of) is connected to "jaza," meaning: a recompense arising from arrogance, and in it there is the sense of mockery. It is permissible that it means "in exchange for," and the more likely view is that it means "after." It is also said that it means "in," but this is nothing, and the present tense is used instead of the past to make the past present, because it is wondrous.]

This is indicated by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-qad tabb." It is narrated that when the verse ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen﴾ was revealed, he (ﷺ) climbed al-Safa and said: "Ya sabahah!" So the people gathered to him from every direction. He said: "O sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, O sons of Fihr, if I told you that there were horsemen at the foot of this mountain, would you believe me?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." Abu Lahab said: "Ruin to you! Is it for this that you gathered us?" [Agreed upon from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both.] Then this was revealed.

If you ask: why did He use the kunya for him, when the kunya is a mark of honour? I say: in this there are three aspects. The first: that he was well known by the kunya rather than the name; a man may be known by one of the two, and for this reason the kunya is applied to the name, or the name to the kunya, as an explanatory apposition. When it was intended to make him notorious through the curse, and for it to remain a mark upon him, the better known of his two names was mentioned. This is supported by the reading of one who read "yadan Abu Lahab." [Mahmud said: "This is supported by the reading of one who read 'yadan Abu Lahab'." Ahmad said: In this there is evidence, because the nominative is the earliest and first of the case-endings. Do you not see that they only preserved the form in which the name became well known, which was its first state?] As it is said: "Ali ibn Abu Talib" and "Mu'awiya ibn Abu Sufyan," so that nothing in it is altered and confuses the listener. Also, Lafleh ibn Qasim, the amir of Mecca, had two sons, one named 'Abd Allah with a genitive, and the other 'Abd Allah with an accusative. There was in Mecca a man called 'Abd Allah with a kasra on the dal, known only in this way. The second: his name was 'Abd al-'Uzza, and he was turned away from it to his kunya. The third: since he was among the people of the Fire and his destination was a fire of flame, his condition matched his kunya, so he was worthy of being mentioned by it. It is said "Abu Lahab," just as one says "Abu al-Sharr" for the wicked and "Abu al-Khayr" for the good; and as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave the kunya "Abu Safra" to Abu al-Muhallab, because of the yellowness in his face. It is also said he was given this kunya because of the flame and brightness of his cheeks, so it is permissible that he be mentioned by it in mockery of him and of his boasting in it. It is also read "Abi Lahab" with sukun, and this is from altering proper names, like the saying "Shams ibn Malik" with a damma.

"Ma aghna" is an interrogative in the sense of denial, and its place is accusative or negation. "Wa ma kasaba" is nominative. "Ma" is either relative or verbal-masdariyya, meaning: "and what he acquired" or "and his acquiring." The meaning: his wealth did not benefit him, nor what he acquired by his wealth, that is, the capital and the profits; or his livestock and what he gained from their offspring and their benefits. He had a large herd [Qawl: "wa kana dha sabaya" — in the Qamus, from its entries: abundant wealth and offspring, camels with young and sheep whose offspring increased. "Al-talid" is the old, and "al-tarif" is the newly acquired (ʿ)]. Or his wealth which he inherited from his father and that which he acquired by himself. Or his inherited and his newly acquired wealth. And from Ibn 'Abbas: what his son acquired.

It is related that the sons of Abu Lahab brought their dispute to him, and they fought, so he stood up to restrain them, but one of them pushed him and he fell. He became angry and said: "Remove from me the wicked acquisition!" From this is his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him: "The best that a man eats is from his own earnings, and his child is from his earnings." From Qatada: his deed which he thought was something, like the Exalted's saying: ﴿And We shall turn to what they did of deeds﴾. It is narrated that he used to say: "If what my nephew says is true, I will ransom myself from it with my wealth and my children."

It is also said she used to walk about with slander. Those who walk about with tale-bearing and sow discord among people are called "one who carries firewood between them," meaning: she kindles strife between them and breeds evil. He said:

"Of the white ones, not found upon the back of a saddled camel, nor walking among the tribe with moist firewood."

[It was recited by Ya'qub. "Al-bayad" is a metaphor for freedom from causes of blame. "Tasid" is from hunting, meaning finding and perceiving; its form is yaftaʿil, so the ta of the iftaʿal was changed to ta' by analogy. Some narrate it as "yadhid," and others as "yadtid," with the letters ḍād, both meaning from enmity; let us consider the second, for the dal in it should be doubled, so perhaps he lightened it for necessity. "Al-lāma" is blame and its cause; he likened her to the mount which its rider is accustomed to riding along the path of metonymy, so he attributed to her a back as imaginative representation of that. Another narration has "bi-l-khaṭar" in place of "al-hatab," which is wood, and the firewood with which one is struck, and the meaning is slander; this is figuratively applied to it, by the common quality of the rising of the disliked, because moist firewood when fire is kindled in it gives much smoke. Another narration: "lam yuḍaddid" and "lam yamshi" with a ya, as an attribute of a masculine.]

He made it moist to indicate the smoke, which is an increase in evil. "Wa-l-hatab" is raised as a conjunction upon the pronoun in "sayaslá": that is, "he and his wife shall be burned." "Fi jidiha" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, or, if it is a beginning, then "fi jidiha" is the predicate. It is read "hammalat al-hatab" in the accusative as a curse, and I prefer this reading; and it is said that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to curse Umm Jamil..." "And a strong rope of camels' hair... "

[The verses: "If it pleases you to have water without driving the camels by which water is drawn, then hasten with a bucket like the bucket of Tariq. And a rope strongly twisted of camels' hair, not of teeth nor of... nor weak ones whose marrow has gone." This is for 'Umara ibn Tariq. He says: if it pleases you to draw water while you are not driving the camels upon which water is drawn, then hasten to the water of a well with a great bucket like the bucket of my father Tariq. Others said: "al-zahiq" here means "departing," and it is genitive by conjunction, meaning: nor weak ones whose marrow... "What did you intend by insulting me and disparaging me, or what do you reproach me with, the carrier of firewood? A fair woman whose forehead is broad in glory, she was the offspring of an elder of noble lineage."

[This is the reproach of al-Fadl ibn al-'Abbas ibn 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab. "Hammalat al-hatab" was the wife of Abu Lahab, and so she was his grandmother. "Al-ghara'" is the white one. "Al-shadikha" is the broad, and that is a metaphor for prominence and elevated rank. "Al-salila" is one born of another, and "the elder" refers to her father Harb, for she was Umm Jamil, sister of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb. She was one-eyed, and died strangled by her rope with which she carried firewood. It is also said that carrying firewood is a metaphor for stirring up strife, because she was a slanderer. "Ila shatmi" is connected to a deleted element or to "aradta," by way of tadmin, meaning: "what did you intend, inclining toward insulting me," or "joined with it to my insult." Or: "what did you intend by my insult, or with my insult? Did you intend that you are noble with no fault in you?" It is permissible that "ila" means "min," as the grammarians said, citing for it the saying:

"You say, when I have raised the saddle-bags above her, 'Give drink, so that Ibn Ahmar is not satisfied with it.'"

It is also possible that it is for accompaniment, as they said also concerning the Exalted's saying: ﴿and do not devour their wealth along with your wealth﴾. "Ta'ayyar" is originally "tata'ayyar," with one of the two ta's deleted. "As for the slanderous grandmother, it is not fitting to avoid this." Another narration: "thaqib al-hasab." The meaning: that his lineage is noble, as if he were included among the ancestors of the foremost. "Or walking among the people, and her disparagement now, with the elevation of her station formerly, is more severe in humiliation."]

It may also be that the meaning is: her condition will be in the fire of Hell in the form in which she was when she carried the bundle of thorns; so there will always be upon her back a bundle of firewood of the Fire, from the tree of Zaqqum or from the dari', and upon her neck a rope of what is twisted of chains of Fire, just as every criminal is punished according to what matches his condition in his crime.

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the Surah of Tabbat, I hope that God will not gather him and Abu Lahab in one house."

[Narrated by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]

And a rope strongly twisted of camels' hair, not of teeth nor of... nor weak ones whose marrow has gone." This is for 'Umara ibn Tariq. He says: if it pleases you to draw water while you are not driving the camels upon which water is drawn, then hasten to the water of a well with a great bucket like the bucket of my father Tariq. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 111, verses 1–5:

Makkiyya, and its verses are 5 [revealed after al-Fatiha]. In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.

Al-tabab (destruction, ruin). From it comes their saying: "Ashabah umm tabbah," meaning: a woman ruined by old age and incapacity. The meaning is: "May his hands perish," because, as it is narrated, he took a stone to throw at the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he perished entirely. Or, his hands were made to perish. What is meant is the perishing of his whole person, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿because of what your hands have sent forward﴾. The meaning of "wa tabba" is: that occurred and came about, as in the poet's saying:

"May God repay him with the worst of his recompense, the recompense of the snarling dogs, and he has indeed done it."

[It is as if he had done him a good turn, so he repaid him with evil, and so he invoked against him by saying: "May God repay him with the worst of his recompense." "The recompense of the dogs" is an apposition to "the worst of his recompense," and the pronoun in "his recompense" refers to God, or to the man invoked against. "The recompense of the snarling dogs" means: stoning them. It is also narrated as "al-'adiyat" with a dal in place of the waw. "And he has indeed done it" means: God did that recompense in reality, since He brought it about. In it is one of the types of rhetorical ornament:

Al-ruju' (retraction), which is returning to the preceding speech by annulling it for a purpose, because the logic of an invocation is that the thing invoked for has not occurred, so he annulled it with his saying "and he has indeed done it." It is also narrated, in place of the first half-line: "May his Lord repay 'Adi ibn Hatim on my behalf." The pronoun "his Lord" refers to Hatim, even though it is delayed in wording and rank, out of necessity; al-Akhfash, Ibn Jinni and Ibn Malik permitted it in a broad sense, because the object had been placed first owing to the strong demand of the verb for it. It is also said that the returning pronoun is the recompense understood from "jaza." It is also narrated, in place of the first half-line as well: "May God repay 'Abs, the 'Abs of the family of Bughayd." This is a well-known tribe, and the poet is probably someone else. What some commentators on the shawahid of al-Jami have related, that 'Adi ibn Hatim was a man who had built a palace for al-Nu'man ibn Imru' al-Qays on the outskirts of Kufa, and he was impressed by it, so he asked him: "Have you built one like it?" He said: "No, and I built it on a stone; if it fell, the palace would fall," so he threw him from its top and he fell dead, is an error. The correct view is that this story actually happened to Sinimmar, who is mentioned in the saying:

"His sons repaid Abu al-Ghaylan, out of arrogance, and good deeds are repaid as Sinimmar was repaid."

For 'Adi ibn Hatim was a companion from the core of the Arabs; and the pronoun "his sons" refers to Abu al-Ghaylan with a kasra. Sinimmar is with two kasras and then a shadda.

"'An" (from/on account of) is connected to "jaza," meaning: a recompense arising from arrogance, and in it there is the sense of mockery. It is permissible that it means "in exchange for," and the more likely view is that it means "after." It is also said that it means "in," but this is nothing, and the present tense is used instead of the past to make the past present, because it is wondrous.]

This is indicated by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-qad tabb." It is narrated that when the verse ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen﴾ was revealed, he (ﷺ) climbed al-Safa and said: "Ya sabahah!" So the people gathered to him from every direction. He said: "O sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, O sons of Fihr, if I told you that there were horsemen at the foot of this mountain, would you believe me?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." Abu Lahab said: "Ruin to you! Is it for this that you gathered us?" [Agreed upon from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both.] Then this was revealed.

If you ask: why did He use the kunya for him, when the kunya is a mark of honour? I say: in this there are three aspects. The first: that he was well known by the kunya rather than the name; a man may be known by one of the two, and for this reason the kunya is applied to the name, or the name to the kunya, as an explanatory apposition. When it was intended to make him notorious through the curse, and for it to remain a mark upon him, the better known of his two names was mentioned. This is supported by the reading of one who read "yadan Abu Lahab." [Mahmud said: "This is supported by the reading of one who read 'yadan Abu Lahab'." Ahmad said: In this there is evidence, because the nominative is the earliest and first of the case-endings. Do you not see that they only preserved the form in which the name became well known, which was its first state?] As it is said: "Ali ibn Abu Talib" and "Mu'awiya ibn Abu Sufyan," so that nothing in it is altered and confuses the listener. Also, Lafleh ibn Qasim, the amir of Mecca, had two sons, one named 'Abd Allah with a genitive, and the other 'Abd Allah with an accusative. There was in Mecca a man called 'Abd Allah with a kasra on the dal, known only in this way. The second: his name was 'Abd al-'Uzza, and he was turned away from it to his kunya. The third: since he was among the people of the Fire and his destination was a fire of flame, his condition matched his kunya, so he was worthy of being mentioned by it. It is said "Abu Lahab," just as one says "Abu al-Sharr" for the wicked and "Abu al-Khayr" for the good; and as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave the kunya "Abu Safra" to Abu al-Muhallab, because of the yellowness in his face. It is also said he was given this kunya because of the flame and brightness of his cheeks, so it is permissible that he be mentioned by it in mockery of him and of his boasting in it. It is also read "Abi Lahab" with sukun, and this is from altering proper names, like the saying "Shams ibn Malik" with a damma.

"Ma aghna" is an interrogative in the sense of denial, and its place is accusative or negation. "Wa ma kasaba" is nominative. "Ma" is either relative or verbal-masdariyya, meaning: "and what he acquired" or "and his acquiring." The meaning: his wealth did not benefit him, nor what he acquired by his wealth, that is, the capital and the profits; or his livestock and what he gained from their offspring and their benefits. He had a large herd [Qawl: "wa kana dha sabaya" — in the Qamus, from its entries: abundant wealth and offspring, camels with young and sheep whose offspring increased. "Al-talid" is the old, and "al-tarif" is the newly acquired (ʿ)]. Or his wealth which he inherited from his father and that which he acquired by himself. Or his inherited and his newly acquired wealth. And from Ibn 'Abbas: what his son acquired.

It is related that the sons of Abu Lahab brought their dispute to him, and they fought, so he stood up to restrain them, but one of them pushed him and he fell. He became angry and said: "Remove from me the wicked acquisition!" From this is his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him: "The best that a man eats is from his own earnings, and his child is from his earnings." From al-Dahhak: what his wealth and his wicked deeds did not benefit him, meaning his scheming in enmity against the Messenger of God (ﷺ). From Qatada: his deed which he thought was something, like the Exalted's saying: ﴿And We shall turn to what they did of deeds﴾. It is narrated that he used to say: "If what my nephew says is true, I will ransom myself from it with my wealth and my children."

"Sayaslá" is read with a fatha and with a damma on the ya, lightened and intensified. The sin is for threat, meaning: it is certain to happen, though its time may be delayed.

"Wa-imra'atuhu" is Umm Jamil bint Harb, sister of Abu Sufyan, and she used to carry a bundle of thorns and tribulus [Qawl: "min al-shawk wa-l-hasak." In the Sihah: "al-hasak" is the tribulus of al-sa'dan, and "al-sa'dan" is a thorny plant; this plant has thorns, so it is called hasak al-sa'dan (ʿ)] and sa'dan, and she would scatter them at night on the path of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is also said she used to walk about with slander. Those who walk about with tale-bearing and sow discord among people are called "one who carries firewood between them," meaning: she kindles strife between them and breeds evil. He said:

"Of the white ones, not found upon the back of a saddled camel, nor walking among the tribe with moist firewood."

[It was recited by Ya'qub. "Al-bayad" is a metaphor for freedom from causes of blame. "Tasid" is from hunting, meaning finding and perceiving; its form is yaftaʿil, so the ta of the iftaʿal was changed to ta' by analogy. Some narrate it as "yadhid," and others as "yadtid," with the letters ḍād, both meaning from enmity; let us consider the second, for the dal in it should be doubled, so perhaps he lightened it for necessity. "Al-lāma" is blame and its cause; he likened her to the mount which its rider is accustomed to riding along the path of metonymy, so he attributed to her a back as imaginative representation of that. Another narration has "bi-l-khaṭar" in place of "al-hatab," which is wood, and the firewood with which one is struck, and the meaning is slander; this is figuratively applied to it, by the common quality of the rising of the disliked, because moist firewood when fire is kindled in it gives much smoke. Another narration: "lam yuḍaddid" and "lam yamshi" with a ya, as an attribute of a masculine.]

He made it moist to indicate the smoke, which is an increase in evil. "Wa-l-hatab" is raised as a conjunction upon the pronoun in "sayaslá": that is, "he and his wife shall be burned." "Fi jidiha" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, or, if it is a beginning, then "fi jidiha" is the predicate. It is read "hammalat al-hatab" in the accusative as a curse, and I prefer this reading; and it is said that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to curse Umm Jamil..." It is also read "hammalatun li-l-hatab," and "hammalatun lil-hatab" with tanwin, in the nominative and accusative. It is also read "wa-marratuhu" with diminutive.
